settings.title: start with the craft
settings.body: Workshop induction, tool discipline and a first small build in bamboo, so nobody touches a frame until the basics are second nature.

settings.title: learn the bike
settings.body: Bicycle theory: geometry, how a frame carries load, what every part does. The week ends with each Maker pitching a bike company of their own.

settings.title: build the frame
settings.body: Three weeks at the jig: measure, mitre, bond and finish a full bamboo frame, quality-checked at every gate, then components fitted and a supervised test ride.

settings.title: the bike that goes home
settings.body: The balance-bike course follows: each Maker designs and builds a child's bike, writes its user guide and a personal message, and hands it over on family visit day.

sq ft dedicated workshop at our flagship site

settings.why_body_2: Ministry of Justice research found prisoners who receive family visits are 39% less likely to reoffend (Lord Farmer Review, 2017). And with just 20% of prison-leavers in work six weeks after release nationally (MoJ, 2024–25), the skills matter as much as the bond. Build to Bond is built on both: real skills, an assessed qualification, and a stronger family bond at the finish line.
settings.sites_body: Build to Bond is established across four UK prison sites, at different delivery stages — with a self-delivery model that trains prison staff and peer instructors to run the workshop.
settings.sites_partner: Delivered under direct contracts with HMPPS and private operators

settings.film_caption: Three minutes, subtitled. Filmed inside HMP Lowdham Grange by the prison's Inside Media Department. Makers are not identifiable.
settings.steps_lede: Eighteen hours a week in the workshop. Every Maker builds a full bamboo frame from raw tubes, then designs and builds the balance bike that goes home with their child.
settings.path1_body: The core course. From raw bamboo to a finished frame: measuring, mitring, bonding, paint and finishing, components and a test ride, with a portfolio assessed against OCN Level 2 (centre course 1130735). 108 contact hours per Maker.
settings.path2_tag: course two · the bike that goes home
settings.path2_title: Introduction to Product Design and Manufacture (Bamboo Balance Bike)
settings.path2_body: Makers design and build a child's balance bike, write its user guide and a personal message, and present it on family visit day. Opt-in and trauma-informed throughout. OCN Level 2, centre course 1131207.
settings.path3_body: Makers who finish can help teach the next cohort. More than ten have, alongside the 14 prison staff we have trained to run the workshop themselves.
settings.recog_c: National Justice Museum, Working Through It exhibition, 2026
settings.hero_lede: Build to Bond is a six-week bamboo bike-building course inside prison workshops. Makers learn real manufacturing skills, work towards an OCN Level 2, and finish by handing a bike they built to their own child.
settings.story_body_1: We built a new kind of training for prisons. If school felt like failing, this is maths, measurement, design and engineering you can do with your hands, and it ends with something you can hold. Inside a working prison workshop, small cohorts of Makers measure, mitre and bond bamboo frames from raw tubes: the same craft we have taught in our London workshop since 2012.
settings.story_body_2: It is not just bikes. Makers learn design theory, tolerances and jig work, bicycle mechanics, painting and finishing, and how to check their own work against a standard. Every session builds a portfolio of evidence towards an OCN Level 2, assessed as they go.
settings.why_body_1: The finished build is a child's balance bike. On family visit day, the Maker hands it over themselves. For many it is the first thing they have ever made, given to the person who matters most.
settings.steps_title: six weeks to a frame. then the bike that goes home.
settings.cs_lede: Every story from the prison programme, in their own words and ours: the flagship site, a new workshop opening, the minister, the press, and the students who redesigned the course.
